procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated June 25, 1968, of the Kerala High Court in Criminal M.P. Nos. 175, 177, and 179 of 1968, which confirmed the Trial Court's permission for the Public Prosecutor to withdraw from the prosecution under s. 494, Cr. P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. Respondents were committed to trial before the Sessions Court for offences of forgery, cheating, etc.
2. They challenged the committal order, but the High Court held that there was a prima facie case.
3. The trial judge split up the charges, and this was questioned, but the High Court held that there was no illegality.
4. The Public Prosecutor applied under s. 494, Cr. P.C., under instructions from the Government, for permission to withdraw from the prosecution.
5. The Trial Court granted permission, and the High Court confirmed the order in revision (Criminal M.P. Nos. 175, 177, and 179 of 1968).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the permission granted by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High Court, and directed that the trial proceed in accordance with the law.

directions: The permission granted by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High Court in Revision is set aside.
The trial do proceed in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the executive, including a Minister or the Government, has the power to interfere with a pending prosecution by ordering its withdrawal and usurping the functions of the court.

facts: In several cases reviewed by the court, Public Prosecutors, acting under instructions from the government, applied under Section 494 of the Criminal Procedure Code to withdraw from pending prosecutions.
The reasons given for withdrawal often included government policy, expediency, delay in trial, or the expense of securing witnesses.

In one instance, the government called for the record of a pending case from the magistrate, held it for six months, and then instructed the prosecutor to seek withdrawal, an action the High Court deemed "quite illegal and utterly improper."
law: Section 494 of the Criminal Procedure Code states that a Public Prosecutor may, with the consent of the Court, withdraw from the prosecution of any person before a judgment is pronounced.
The court's consent is a mandatory prerequisite for any withdrawal under this section.
The court cited precedents establishing that the executive does not have the power to usurp the functions of the court or take a case out of its control while it is pending.
application: The Supreme Court clarified that the power to withdraw a prosecution is not an absolute executive power. The critical element is the consent of the court, which cannot be granted as a mere formality.
The court has a duty to scrutinize the reasons for the withdrawal. It must be satisfied that the withdrawal serves the "administration of justice" and is not sought for extraneous reasons.

Reasons such as general government policy or expediency, unconnected with the merits of the case, are not valid grounds for withdrawal. The court must ensure that offenses do not go unpunished simply because the government directs the prosecutor to withdraw.

The court must exercise its own independent discretion and not simply permit a withdrawal because the government has ordered it. If a magistrate allows a withdrawal merely in consequence of a government order without applying their own mind, a higher court will interfere.

Therefore, any attempt by the executive to order a withdrawal and bypass the court's independent judgment is considered an interference with the course of justice and a usurpation of the judicial function.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that the executive has the power to interfere with a pending prosecution by ordering its withdrawal. It held that while the Public Prosecutor initiates the withdrawal request, the court retains ultimate control. The court must independently grant its consent only if it is satisfied that the withdrawal is in the interest of justice, thereby preventing the executive from usurping the court's function.

issue.issue_text: Whether the fact that the alleged acts may give rise to both civil and criminal liability is a sufficient ground to permit withdrawal from the criminal prosecution, especially when a prima facie case has been established.

facts: The respondents were facing criminal prosecution for offences including forgery and cheating.
The High Court had previously held on two occasions that a prima facie case existed against the respondents.

The Public Prosecutor sought permission to withdraw from the prosecution, arguing, among other things, that the transaction was of a civil nature, arose from a contract, and had been the subject of a civil suit.
law: The fact that an act may give rise to both civil and criminal liability is not, by itself, a justification for withdrawing from a criminal prosecution.
Withdrawal on this ground is only permissible if the matter before the criminal court is of a "purely civil nature."
application: The Court applied the principle that concurrent civil and criminal liability does not justify withdrawal from prosecution.
It emphasized that a prima facie case for criminal charges had already been established in prior proceedings, which indicated the matter was not purely civil.
The Court explicitly stated that while the respondents' acts might make them liable under both civil and criminal law, this fact does not justify granting permission to withdraw the criminal case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the existence of parallel civil liability is not a sufficient ground to permit withdrawal from a criminal prosecution, particularly when a prima facie criminal case has already been found to exist.

issue.issue_text: Whether delay in the trial or the expenditure involved in the prosecution are, by themselves, proper grounds for a court to grant permission to withdraw from the case.

facts: The Public Prosecutor applied for permission to withdraw from a prosecution, citing several grounds.

Among these grounds were the long delay in the trial (the case was registered in 1963 and had not yet begun) and the heavy expenses the State would incur in securing evidence from witnesses in far-off places like Bombay and Calcutta.
law: The power to grant permission for withdrawal from a prosecution should be exercised in the interest of the administration of justice.
Permission should not be granted on grounds that are extraneous to the interests of justice.
application: The Court found the grounds of delay and expenditure to be "flimsy" and insufficient to justify withdrawal.
Regarding the delay, the Court noted that it was caused by the accused themselves filing several revision petitions, and such a delay cannot be used as a ground for withdrawal.
Regarding the expenditure, the Court found there was no material evidence to show what the actual amount would be or how many witnesses would need to be called from distant locations.
The Court stated that prima facie, neither of these grounds, nor their cumulative effect, could justify the withdrawal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that neither delay in the trial nor the expenditure involved in the prosecution are, by themselves, proper grounds for a court to grant permission to withdraw from a case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the executive, including a Minister or the Government, has the power to interfere with a pending prosecution by ordering its withdrawal and usurping the functions of the court.
appellant_arguments: The Public Prosecutor alone must decide to withdraw from a prosecution under Sec. 494 Criminal Procedure Code, without any reference to or direction from the State Government.
In this case, the Public Prosecutor did not exercise independent judgment but was directed by the State Government to seek permission for withdrawal.
Note: The appellant's advocate later conceded during the argument that there was no force in this contention.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's counter-argument, but their position was that the application for withdrawal was valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the fact that the alleged acts may give rise to both civil and criminal liability is a sufficient ground to permit withdrawal from the criminal prosecution, especially when a prima facie case has been established.
appellant_arguments: Permission to withdraw should not have been granted because the High Court had previously determined that there was a prima facie case for the trial to proceed.
respondent_arguments: The withdrawal was justified because the transaction relating to the offence arose out of a contract and was of a civil nature.

arguments.issue_text: Whether delay in the trial or the expenditure involved in the prosecution are, by themselves, proper grounds for a court to grant permission to withdraw from the case.
appellant_arguments: The grounds of delay and expense disclosed by the Public Prosecutor were insufficient to justify granting permission to withdraw.
respondent_arguments: The withdrawal was justified due to the enormous delay in proceeding with the trial.
Securing evidence from witnesses in far-off places would involve heavy expense for the State, justifying the withdrawal.

cases.case_name: The State of Bihar v. Ram Narash Pandey
cases.principle: Although Section 494 does not specify the grounds for a Public Prosecutor's application to withdraw from prosecution, the court granting consent must satisfy itself that the prosecutor's executive function has not been improperly exercised and is not an attempt to interfere with the normal course of justice for illegitimate reasons or purposes.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The court's discretion to grant permission for the withdrawal of a prosecution cannot be based on flimsy grounds such as the potential for acquittal, delay attributable to the accused, or the expense of the trial, especially after a prima facie case has been found to exist.
obiter: Section 494 of the Code is not in pari materia with s. 333 under which the Advocate General may enter a nolle prosequi.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: It is clear that prima facie none of these grounds or even the cumulative effect of all these grounds would justify the withdrawal from the prosecution. It m~y be that the acts of the Respondent may make them both liable under the Civil law as well a, under the Criminal law but it does l)Ot justify either the seeking of the permission to withdraw from the prosecution or granting of it unless the matter before the Criminal Court is of a purely civil nature. The accused in this case have been committed to trial before the Sessions Court for offences of forgery, cheating, etc. They challenged the committal order but the High Court held that. there was a prima facie case. Thereafter, the trial judge split up the char&es and this was •!lain questioned but the High Court held that there was no illegality.
legal_tests_applied: The essential consideration which is implicit in the grant of the power is that it should be in the interest of administration of justice which may be either that it will not be able to produce sufficient evidence to sustain the charge or that subsequent information before prosecuting agency would falsify the prosecutioJJ evidence or any other similar circumstances.

The Court, while considering the request to grant permission, should not do so as a formality for the mere asking. It may grant permission only if it is satisfied on the materials placed before it that the grant of it subserves the administration of justice and that the permission was not sought covertly with an ulterior purpose unconnected with the vindication of the law.

It is the duty of the Court to see that the permission is not sought on grounds extraneous to the interests of justice or that offences against the State do not go unpunished merely because the Government as a matter of general policy or expediency unconnected with its duty to prosecute offenders directs a Public Prosecutor to withdraw from the prosecution.
why_respondent_won: The fact that the alleged acts may give rise to both civil and criminal liability is not a justification for withdrawal, especially when the High Court had previously found that there was a prima facie criminal case against the accused.
The delay in the trial was caused by the respondents themselves filing several revisions, and therefore the delay by itself cannot be made a ground for according permission to withdraw.

The ground of expenditure was not substantiated with any material to show what amount would be involved or how many witnesses would be required. In any case, the expenditure involved is not the sole criterion for granting permission.
The court found the cumulative grounds presented for withdrawal—civil nature, delay, and expense—to be 'flimsy and do not justify the granting of permission to withdraw from the prosecution.'
policy_considerations: The wide and general powers conferred under Sec. 494 on the Public Prosecutor to withdraw from the prosecution... have to be exercised by him... in furtherance of, rather than as a hindrance to the object of the law.
It is not an attempt to interfere with the normal course of justice for illegitimate reasons or purposes.
The executive does not have the power to usurp the functions of the Court or to take the case out of the seisin of the Magistrate before whom it is pending for trial.
